**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit
hyperboloid.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline in the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with four-velocity $U = dx/d\tau$ and four-acceleration $A = dU/d\tau$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), so that $\eta(U,U) = -c^2$ and $\eta(U,A) = 0$ pointwise, and $A(\tau)$ is spacelike whenever it is nonzero ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] (a),(b)).

**(a) Definition.** The **proper acceleration** of $x$ at the parameter value $\tau$ is the real number

$$a(\tau) := \sqrt{\eta(A(\tau),A(\tau))},$$

the nonnegative square root of [[def-rational-power]]. This is well defined for every $\tau \in I$. Indeed, fix an inertial chart of $A$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); since $x$ is $C^2$, the component functions of $A$ are continuous, and $\eta(A,A)$ is a sum of products of continuous component functions, hence continuous, by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. If $A(\tau) = 0$ then $\eta(A,A) = 0$ at $\tau$, and if $A(\tau) \neq 0$ then $A(\tau)$ is spacelike and $\eta(A,A) > 0$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); in both cases the argument of the square root is nonnegative, so $a(\tau)$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number for every $\tau \in I$. With the SI coordinate and unit conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], in which $x^0 = c t$ with $t$ in seconds and the spatial coordinates are in metres while $\eta$ has the dimensionless matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ in an inertial chart, the components of $A$ carry the unit metre per second squared and $\eta(A,A)$ carries the unit $(\text{metre per second squared})^2$, so $a$ carries the unit metre per second squared. The worldline is **uniformly accelerated** when $a$ is constant on $I$.

**(b) Agreement with the acceleration of a congruence.** Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ and let $n : \Omega \to V$ be an observer congruence with acceleration field $a_{\mathrm{cg}} := \nabla_n n$, where $\nabla$ is the flat covariant derivative of [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]] (b)). If $x$ is a flow line of $n$ and $U = c n$ along $x$, then $A = c^2 a_{\mathrm{cg}}$ along $x$: the derivative along the worldline of the field $n$ is the covariant derivative $\nabla_{dx/d\tau} n = \nabla_{cn} n = c \nabla_n n = c\, a_{\mathrm{cg}}$, by the defining properties of the flat covariant derivative along curves ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] (d)), so $A = d(c n)/d\tau = c\, \nabla_{dx/d\tau} n = c^2 a_{\mathrm{cg}}$. Consequently $a = c^2 \sqrt{\eta(a_{\mathrm{cg}},a_{\mathrm{cg}})}$ along $x$: the proper acceleration is $c^2$ times the magnitude of the congruence acceleration. In particular the proper acceleration of a congruence worldline is determined by the congruence field alone, and such a worldline is uniformly accelerated exactly when $\eta(a_{\mathrm{cg}},a_{\mathrm{cg}})$ is constant along it.

**(c) Reading and scope.** This item defines a quantity of the model and fixes its name, its unit and its physical reading. The model reads $a(\tau)$ as the magnitude that an ideal accelerometer carried along the worldline would register at $\tau$; this ideal-instrument identification is adopted with the model in the same sense as the framework's ideal-clock reading of proper time and is not derived here. No accelerometer response law, calibration, frequency dependence, force law or interaction is specified or asserted; the definition asserts nothing about which bodies follow which worldlines; no measurement outcome and no statistical, uncertainty or empirical claim is made. No choice principle is used.

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]): $A$ is a nonempty affine space over
the $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ with displacement vectors $q-p$ and
translations $v \mapsto p+v$ ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]), and $C^+$
is one of the two connected components of the timelike set
$T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, chosen as the time orientation, with
$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ the other component
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$\overline{C^+}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and
$\overline{C^-}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ for the future and past closed cones.
A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal according to the sign
of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is
not causal, and the causal vectors are exactly the nonzero elements of
$\overline{C^+}\cup\overline{C^-}$.

**The closed cones and their boundaries.** By
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], applied in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$, the closure of the
component $\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ of the timelike set is
$\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ with boundary points exactly $0$ and the nonzero null
vectors of $\overline{C^+}$. Writing $N^+$ and $N^-$ for the sets of nonzero
future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

**The objects fixed by this definition.**

**(a) Causal and chronological reachability.** For events $p,q\in A$ set
$p\le q$ if and only if $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$, and $p<q$ if and only if
$q-p\in C^+$. The first relation is read "$q$ is causally reachable from $p$"
and the second "$q$ is strictly (chronologically) reachable from $p$"; both are
relations on the set of events, and neither is asserted here to have any
property beyond being a relation.

**(b) Futures and pasts.** For an event $p\in A$ set

$$J^+(p):=\{q\in A:p\le q\}=p+\overline{C^+},\qquad I^+(p):=\{q\in A:p<q\}=p+C^+,$$

$$J^-(p):=\{q\in A:q\le p\}=p+\overline{C^-},\qquad I^-(p):=\{q\in A:q<p\}=p+C^-.$$

The displayed equalities hold because $q\in J^+(p)$ says exactly that the
displacement $q-p$ lies in $\overline{C^+}$, that is $q=p+v$ for some
$v\in\overline{C^+}$; here $p+v$ is the affine translation of
[[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]. Since $0\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}$
one has $p\in J^+(p)\cap J^-(p)$, and since $0$ is not timelike one has
$p\notin I^+(p)$ and $p\notin I^-(p)$. The sets
$J^\pm(p)$ and $I^\pm(p)$ are called the causal and chronological future and
past of $p$.

**(c) Causal diamonds.** For events $p,q\in A$ with $p\le q$, the causal diamond
of the ordered pair $(p,q)$ is the set

$$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)=\{r\in A:p\le r\le q\}.$$

The diamond is defined only under the hypothesis $p\le q$; some of its
properties are computed in the examples page of this pair.

**(d) Reachability by future causal paths.** A piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path is a piecewise $C^1$ curve $x:[a,b]\to A$ on a compact interval with
$a<b$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) all of
whose tangents are future causal: at every interior point of every open smooth
piece the tangent $x'(s)$ exists and is future causal, and at every partition
point of $[a,b]$ and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ both one-sided
difference-quotient tangents that exist there exist and are future causal
vectors in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. For events $p,q\in A$, say
that $q$ is reachable from $p$ by a future causal path when $p=q$, or when
$p\ne q$ and there are real numbers $a<b$ and a piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path $x:[a,b]\to A$ with $x(a)=p$ and $x(b)=q$. Write $R^+(p)$ for the set of
events reachable from $p$ in this sense; thus $p\in R^+(p)$ by the first clause.

**(e) Conventions and scope.** All objects above are defined from the affine
structure of $A$, the form $\eta$ and the time orientation alone: no chart, no
choice of origin, no spatial orientation of $V$ and no unit convention enters
their definition. This item asserts no property of these objects
beyond their being well-defined sets and relations: the reflexivity of $\le$ is
part of (b), while the transitivity of $\le$, the identification
$R^+(p)=J^+(p)$, the antisymmetry "$p\le q$ and $q\le p$ imply $p=q$", the
monotonicity of inertial coordinate time along future causal paths and the
invariance of these objects under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps are
proved later on this page and are not used here. No choice principle is used:
all objects are subsets or finite data built from a finite-dimensional real
vector space.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and use
the reachability objects $J^+$, $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$$
be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part $v_s:=v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ of a
vector $v=v^0e_0+v_s$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then:

**(a) Cone description.** $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$,
$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; moreover every $v\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$v\ne 0$ satisfies $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$, and $v$ is future
null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$.

**(b) Finite sums.** If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ lie in $\overline{C^+}$
($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

**(c) Coordinate criterion.** For events $p,q\in A$ put
$D^a:=x^a(q)-x^a(p)$ and $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$. Then: $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only
if $D^0\ge|D_s|$; $q\in I^+(p)$ if and only if $D^0>|D_s|$; $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ if and only if $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$; and for $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ one has $0<D^0$ and $|D_s|\le D^0$. The criteria are stated for the
chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is
$\eta$-orthonormal with future first vector.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed
time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to $\le$, $J^+$ or $I^+$ and
uses no choice principle.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
the reachability objects $\le$, $<$, $J^+$, $I^+$ and $R^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]].

**(a) Displacement of a future causal path.** Let $a<b$ be real numbers and let
$x:[a,b]\to A$ be a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path with $D:=x(b)-x(a)$. Then
$D\in\overline{C^+}$. If $x$ has a future timelike one-sided tangent at some
point of $[a,b]$, then $D\in C^+$. If $x$ is nonconstant, then $D\ne 0$.

**(b) Reachability and straight segments.** $J^+(p)=R^+(p)$, and for $q\ne p$
one has $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only if the straight path
$s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$, $s\in[0,1]$, is a future causal path; moreover
$$I^+(p)=\{q:\text{the straight path from }p\text{ to }q\text{ is future timelike}\} =\{q:q\text{ is reachable from }p\text{ by a piecewise }C^1\text{ future causal path having a future timelike one-sided tangent at some point}\},$$
and $p$ is in neither of these two sets.

**(c) No causal loops.** If $p\le q$ and $q\le p$ then $p=q$; equivalently
there is no nonconstant piecewise $C^1$ future causal path $x:[a,b]\to A$ with
$x(b)=x(a)$.

**(d) Time monotonicity.** For the chart $x$ of every inertial frame and every
piecewise $C^1$ future causal path $y:[a,b]\to A$, the composition $x^0\circ y$
is nondecreasing, and if $y$ is nonconstant on a subinterval $[a',b']$ of
$[a,b]$ then $(x^0\circ y)(b')>(x^0\circ y)(a')$; in particular every inertial
frame agrees that a nonconstant future causal path does not go backwards in
coordinate time.

**(e) Straight-worldline maximum.** Let $p,q$ be events with $q\in I^+(p)$, put
$D:=q-p$ and $T:=\sqrt{-\eta(D,D)}>0$. Then for every piecewise $C^1$ future
timelike worldline $y:[a,b]\to A$ with $y(a)=p$ and $y(b)=q$, the elapsed
proper time
$$\Delta\tau(y)=c^{-1}\sum_i\int_{(a_i,b_i)}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')},$$
defined by the finite improper-piece sum of
[[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]] on the weak $C^1$ pieces
$a=a_1<b_1=a_2<\dots<b_m=b$, is at most $T/c$; equality holds if and only if
the image of $y$ is the straight segment from $p$ to $q$ and $y$ traverses it
with a strictly increasing time coordinate, that is, $y$ is a strictly
increasing reparametrization of $s\mapsto p+sD$.

**(f) Invariance.** For every proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map $F$ of the
model one has $F(J^+(p))=J^+(F(p))$ and $F(I^+(p))=I^+(F(p))$ for every event
$p$, and $p\le q$ if and only if $F(p)\le F(q)$ for all events $p,q$.

**(g) Scope.** The theorem concerns the affine model: it attaches no physical
interpretation to $\le$, $J^+$, $I^+$ and $R^+$, asserts nothing about partial
differential equations, propagation of particular fields or differentiability
beyond piecewise $C^1$, and uses no choice principle.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $I$ be an order-convex subset of
$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
model is a map $x : I \to A$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.

Adopt the ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $x:I\to A$ be a future timelike worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function $\tau$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]), and let $s_-<s_+$ be parameter values in $I$. Suppose an event $q$ and the events $e_-:=x(s_-)$, $e_+:=x(s_+)$ satisfy: $q-e_-$ is future null and $e_+-q$ is future null ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Under the adopted ideal-light assumption an ideal ray is emitted at $e_-$, reaches $q$, and an ideal ray emitted at $q$ reaches $e_+$; the event $q$ is idealized as an instantaneous reflection that changes nothing else. The **radar protocol** of the observer assigns to $q$

(i) the **radar time** $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q):=\tfrac12\bigl(\tau(s_-)+\tau(s_+)\bigr)$, the ideal clock's reading midway between emission and reception, and

(ii) the **radar distance** $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q):=\tfrac{c}{2}\bigl(\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)\bigr)$, half the round-trip light time multiplied by $c$.

Two events measured by the same observer are **radar-simultaneous** when their radar times agree. The assignment does not change under increasing reparametrizations of the observer's worldline, because the proper-time function does not ([[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]).

**Conventions and scope.** (a) The protocol is a definition of an operational assignment conditional on the existence of the emission, reflection and reception events, and it assumes an available ideal reflector and ideal apparatus. (b) The split of the round trip into a "time" and a "distance" uses the symmetric convention in which half of the round-trip time is assigned to the outgoing and half to the returning segment; the protocol determines the round-trip quantity $\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)$ operationally, while the derived one-way assignment is a convention and does not measure a one-way light speed independently of a synchronization convention. (c) Nothing is claimed about accelerated observers, dispersive or absorbing media, finite-resolution apparatus, global single-valuedness or detector models, and no measurement outcome, statistical inference or empirical comparison is asserted.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $n\in V$ be future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

**(a) Rest space.** The **rest space** of $n$ is the hyperplane $n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$; by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c) it is a three-dimensional linear subspace on which $\eta$ restricts to a positive-definite symmetric form, and the orthogonal projection onto it is $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$ ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Simultaneity slice.** For $p\in A$ the **simultaneity slice of $p$ relative to $n$** is the affine hyperplane $H(p,n):=p+n^\perp=\{q\in A:\eta(n,q-p)=0\}$; it contains $p$ and is three-dimensional, not a single point.

**(c) Simultaneity relation.** Define $q\sim_nq'$ if and only if $\eta(n,q'-q)=0$, that is, if and only if $q'-q\in n^\perp$. Then $\sim_n$ is an equivalence relation on $A$ whose equivalence classes are exactly the slices $H(p,n)$; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are consequences of $n^\perp$ being a linear subspace and are not physical assumptions.

**(d) Rest distance.** For $p,q$ with $q\in H(p,n)$ define $d_n(p,q):=\sqrt{\eta(q-p,q-p)}$. This is a real number $\ge0$, symmetric in $p,q$, vanishes exactly when $p=q$, and satisfies the triangle inequality on each slice, because the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is a positive-definite inner product.

**(e) Dependence on $n$ and scope.** The relation $\sim_n$ and the slices $H(p,n)$ depend on the chosen future unit timelike vector $n$: an event $q$ with $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ generally has $\eta(n',q-p)\ne0$ for another future unit $n'$ (an explicit witness is given on this page). Simultaneity here is defined relative to a prescribed observer vector and is not an absolute relation. For a congruence $n(\cdot)$ one may form the pointwise slices $H\bigl(p,n(p)\bigr)$; whether these assemble into hypersurfaces is a separate integrability question settled later on this page, and no global foliation is asserted.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

Adopt the assumption that the equations of the specific mechanical and
electromagnetic models developed from this framework are covariant under the
inertial changes of description: each such model equation has the same form
when its events are relabelled by $F$ and its displacements and other tensors
are transformed by $L$.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let
$x:I\to A$ be a curve whose coordinate representation in an inertial chart is
of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]) with
everywhere future timelike coordinate derivative. An **ideal clock** carried
along $x$ reads, between parameters $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

There is no additional acceleration-dependent term in the reading: the reading
depends only on the curve and the interval, not on the acceleration
(**clock hypothesis**). The integrand is a positive continuous function of $s$
on the compact interval $[a,b]$, so the integral is a well-defined Riemann
integral.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are exactly the future
null straight lines

$$\{\,p+\lambda v:\lambda\in\mathbb R\,\},\qquad p\in A,\quad v\in V\ \text{future null},$$

parametrized at $p$ by $\lambda=0$. In every inertial chart $x$, such a ray has

$$x(\lambda)=x(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3),$$

and because $v$ is future null the components satisfy $v^0=\lvert v_{\text{vec}}\rvert>0$
by the orthonormal-coordinate description of the closed cones
([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]): hence the spatial coordinate
velocity of the ray has magnitude $\lvert v_{\text{vec}}\rvert/v^0\cdot c=c$ in
**every** inertial chart, with $x^0=ct$. The adopted conversion constant $c$ is
therefore the same in all inertial charts; its numerical value is an empirical
parameter of the model.

Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following restriction on
signal transmission, called the **causal signal restriction of the model**.

**(i) Causal restriction.** Let $p$ and $q$ be the emission and reception
events of an idealized transmission that carries a signal, where a *signal* is
understood as information, or a physical marker by which a prepared operation
at the emission event is correlated with an observation at the reception event,
within the model. Then the model admits such a transmission only if $q$ lies in
the causal future $J^+(p)$ of $p$
([[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]), that is, only if
the displacement $q-p$ is zero or future causal
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); equivalently, no signal
connects an event with an event outside its closed future light cone.

**(ii) Ideal light.** The ideal vacuum light signals of
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] are the null boundary case of the
restriction: their displacement between emission and reception is future null,
so in the chart of every inertial frame with $x^0=ct$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]) they attain
$|x_s(q)-x_s(p)|=x^0(q)-x^0(p)$.

**(iii) Status.** This is an adopted assumption about the idealized model; it is
not a theorem of the affine geometry of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], it is
not derived here from the other postulates or from any experiment, and it is not
an empirical claim about nature. In particular the framework does not assert
that no physical process whatsoever exceeds $c$, and the question whether any
specified physical process is a signal of this model, and with what reliability
and reach, is left to a separate experimental interface.

**(iv) Explicit non-restriction.** The assumption does not forbid kinematic
patterns in which spacelike-separated events are produced by independent
prearranged mechanisms without any signal or energy transfer between them (for
example a prearranged row of devices triggered in a fixed sequence), and it
imposes no bound on correlations between spacelike-separated events.

**(v) Scope.** The assumption concerns idealized point-like transmission events
in the flat classical model and carries no statistical, apparatus, source or
detector content; no choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: (Chart domain, wedge and boundary.) From [L3], $\Phi$ is a smooth bijection onto $W$ with the stated smooth inverse defined for $x^1>|x^0|$, so the coordinate domain is exactly $W$ and $\rho=0$ is excluded; on $W$ the coordinates satisfy $U=\rho e^{\theta}>0$ and $V=-\rho e^{-\theta}<0$, and conversely $U>0$ and $V<0$ define $W$, since $x^1=(U-V)/2>|x^0|=|U+V|/2$ is equivalent to $U>0,V<0$. The boundary is $x^1=|x^0|$, split into the two half-planes $x^1=x^0\ge0$ (where $V=0$, $U\ge0$) and $x^1=-x^0\ge0$ (where $U=0$, $V\le0$); these are the parts of the full null planes $V=0$ and $U=0$ that bound $W$, while the full planes extend beyond.

(The worldline $O$ and its parametrization.) By [L3] the curve $\theta\mapsto\Phi(\theta,\rho_0,y_0,z_0)$ is a flow line of $n=\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta$ restricted to $\rho=\rho_0$; its tangent with respect to $\theta$ is $\partial_\theta=\rho_0 n$, so by [L4] its four-velocity is $cn$, its proper time satisfies $d\tau=\rho_0\,d\theta/c$, i.e. $\theta=c\tau/\rho_0$ up to an additive constant, and its proper acceleration is $c^2/\rho_0$. Along it, $U=\rho_0e^{\theta}$ and $V=-\rho_0e^{-\theta}$.

(The future null lines of the plane through $O$.) Let $p,q$ be events in the plane $y=y_0$, $z=z_0$ and $w:=q-p$. Since $w^2=w^3=0$, one has $\Delta U:=U(q)-U(p)=w^0+w^1$, $\Delta V:=V(q)-V(p)=w^0-w^1$, and $\Delta U\Delta V=(w^0)^2-(w^1)^2$; hence $w\in\bar C^+$ iff $\Delta U\ge0$, $\Delta V\ge0$ and $\Delta U\Delta V\ge0$, and $w$ is future null iff in addition $\Delta U\Delta V=(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2=0$, i.e. iff either $\Delta V=0<\Delta U$ or $\Delta U=0<\Delta V$. Differentiating $U=\rho e^{\theta}$ and $V=-\rho e^{-\theta}$ along a curve in $W$ gives $dU=e^{\theta}(d\rho+\rho\,d\theta)$ and $dV=-e^{-\theta}(d\rho-\rho\,d\theta)$, so the future null lines through a point of $O$ in the plane are exactly the constant-$U$ lines ($d\theta=-d\rho/\rho$) and the constant-$V$ lines ($d\theta=+d\rho/\rho$).

(The logarithmic inequality.) For $r>0$ with $r\neq1$, the mean value theorem applied to $\log$ on the interval between $1$ and $r$ gives $\log r-\log1=\frac{1}{c}(r-1)$ for some $c$ strictly between $1$ and $r$; since $c>1$ when $r>1$ this gives $\log r<r-1$, and since $0<c<1$ when $0<r<1$ it gives $-\log r>1-r$; equality holds only at $r=1$. In particular $\log2<2-1=1$, and also $e>2$ gives $\log2<\log e=1$ by strict increase of $\log$.

(Causal criteria for the worldline $O$.) For an arbitrary displacement $w$, $w\in\bar C^+$ is equivalent to $\Delta U\ge0$, $\Delta V\ge0$ and $\Delta U\Delta V\ge(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2$: this follows from $w^0=(\Delta U+\Delta V)/2$ and $\eta(w,w)=-\Delta U\Delta V+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2$ and the inertial cone criterion [L5]. (Forward.) Let $q\le p$ with $p$ on $O$, so $w=p-q\in\bar C^+$; then $\Delta V=V(p)-V(q)\ge0$ and $V(p)=-\rho_0e^{-\theta_p}<0$, so $V(q)\le V(p)<0$. Similarly $\Delta U\ge0$ with $U(p)>0$ gives nothing yet, but the same argument with the roles of $U$ and $V$ reversed and the sign of $\rho_0 e^{\theta_p}$ shows $U(q)\le U(p)$; to obtain $U(q)>0$ from $p\le q$ one uses $w=q-p\in\bar C^+$: then $U(q)-U(p)\ge0$ and $U(p)=\rho_0e^{\theta_p}>0$, so $U(q)\ge U(p)>0$; and $V(q)\ge V(p)$ gives no upper bound. (Reverse.) Suppose $V(q)<0$; choose $\theta_p$ with $-\rho_0e^{-\theta_p}>V(q)$, i.e. $V(p)>V(q)$, which is possible because $-\rho_0e^{-\theta_p}\to0^-$ as $\theta_p\to+\infty$; then $\Delta V>0$, and $\Delta U=\rho_0e^{\theta_p}-U(q)$ and $\Delta U\Delta V$ tend to $+\infty$ as $\theta_p\to+\infty$ while the transverse displacement $(y_0-q^2,z_0-q^3)$ is fixed, so for all sufficiently large $\theta_p$ the three general inequalities just established hold and $q\le p$. Similarly, if $U(q)>0$, choose $\theta_p$ very negative so that $U(p)=\rho_0e^{\theta_p}<U(q)$ and $\Delta U>0$, while $\Delta V=V(q)+\rho_0e^{-\theta_p}\to+\infty$; then $\Delta U\Delta V\to+\infty$ and $p\le q$ for all sufficiently negative $\theta_p$. Hence the criteria, and since the construction used only the positivity of $\rho_0$ and the fixed transverse coordinates of the worldline, the same criteria hold for every congruence worldline $\rho=\rho_1$, $y=y_1$, $z=z_1$. The remaining consequences in (ii) follow by evaluating the signs of $U$ and $V$ on the horizon plane, the left wedge ($U<0<V$) and the future and past wedges.

(Limits along $O$ and along the reflector family.) By [L9], $\rho_0e^{-\theta}\to0$ and $\rho_0e^{\theta}\to+\infty$ as $\theta\to+\infty$, while $\rho_0e^{\theta}\to0$ and $\rho_0e^{-\theta}\to+\infty$ as $\theta\to-\infty$; hence along $O$, $V=-\rho_0e^{-\theta}\to0^-$ and $U\to+\infty$ as $\theta\to+\infty$, and $U\to0^+$ with $V\to-\infty$ as $\theta\to-\infty$.

(Clause (iii): the radar geometry.) Suppose first $\rho_m>\rho_0$. The constant-$V$ future null line from $e_-=(\theta_e,\rho_0)$ has $V=-\rho_0e^{-\theta_e}$, and its intersection with $\rho=\rho_m$ is at the unique $\theta_m$ with $-\rho_m e^{-\theta_m}=-\rho_0e^{-\theta_e}$, i.e. $\theta_m=\theta_e+\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)=\theta_e+|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ since $\rho_m>\rho_0$; the return leg must be the constant-$U$ line through $q_m=(\theta_m,\rho_m)$ (the constant-$V$ line leaves $\rho$ increasing), and it meets $\rho=\rho_0$ at the unique $\theta(e_+)$ with $\rho_0e^{\theta(e_+)}=\rho_me^{\theta_m}$, i.e. $\theta(e_+)=\theta_m+\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)=\theta_e+2\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)$. If instead $0<\rho_m<\rho_0$, the same computation with the roles of $U$ and $V$ exchanged, using the two formulas $U=\rho e^{\theta}$ and $V=-\rho e^{-\theta}$, gives $\theta_m=\theta_e+\log(\rho_0/\rho_m)$ and $\theta(e_+)=\theta_m+\log(\rho_0/\rho_m)$, i.e. in both cases $\theta_m=\theta_e+|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ and $\theta(e_+)=\theta_e+2|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ with midpoint $\theta_m$. Uniqueness of $q_m$ and $e_+$ holds because each constant-$U$ or constant-$V$ line meets each of the lines $\rho=\mathrm{const}>0$ exactly once, and $e_-\le q_m$ and $q_m\le e_+$ are future null by step 1.3.

(Clause (i).) Step 1.1 gives the bijection, its domain, the boundary description and the identification of the horizon planes with $V=0$ and $U=0$ on the wedge closure; step 1.3 identifies the two families of future null lines in the plane through $O$ with the constant-$V$ and constant-$U$ lines and their differential equations; step 2.2 gives the asymptotic limits of $U$ and $V$ along $O$.

(Clause (ii).) The two criteria are step 2.1; the stated consequences for the horizon planes, the left wedge and the future and past wedges follow by computing $U$ and $V$ there, using that $x^1<-|x^0|$ gives $U<0$ and $V>0$, $x^0>|x^1|$ gives $U>0,V>0$, and $x^0<-|x^1|$ gives $U<0,V<0$; the horizon interpretations as boundary of the causal past and future of $O$ follow from the two criteria together with the limits of step 2.2, and the invariance in $\rho_1,y_1,z_1$ is the last sentence of step 2.1.

(Clause (iii): the radar assignments and the distance comparison.) By [L6] and step 2.3, the radar time is $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q_m)=(\tau(e_-)+\tau(e_+))/2=(\rho_0/c)\theta_m+\tau_0$, since $\theta=c\tau/\rho_0+\mathrm{const}$ along $O$ by step 1.2, and the radar distance is $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q_m)=c(\tau(e_+)-\tau(e_-))/2=\rho_0|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$; the radar-time level sets in the coaxial family are the sets $\theta_m=\mathrm{const}$, which are exactly the Rindler simultaneity slices because $q_m$ lies on the line $\rho=\rho_m$ at Rindler time $\theta_m$, and these slices are the rest slices of the congruence by [L3]. The rest distance in the slice $\theta=\theta_m$ is $|\rho_m-\rho_0|$ by [L7] and the induced metric $d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$ of [L3]. With $r=\rho_m/\rho_0\neq1$, the radar distance is $\rho_0|\log r|$ and the rest distance is $\rho_0|r-1|$, so by step 1.4 the radar distance is strictly smaller than the rest distance for $r>1$ and strictly larger for $0<r<1$, with equality only in the degenerate case $r=1$ in which both are zero; in particular at $\rho_m=2\rho_0$, $\rho_0\log2<\rho_0$.

(Clause (iv): the restrictions, and the example.) Let $q$ admit a radar triple $e_-,q,e_+$ from $O$; by the ideal-light and signal assumptions of [L1], the emission and reflection legs give $e_-\le q$ and $q\le e_+$ with $e_-,e_+$ on $O$, so by step 2.1's criteria $U(q)>0$ and $V(q)<0$, i.e. $q\in W$; conversely every event with $V\ge0$ fails $q\le p$ for all $p\in O$ and every event with $U\le0$ fails $p\le q$, so those events receive no radar assignment. For the example $q=x^{-1}(2\rho_0,0,y_0,z_0)$: $U(q)=V(q)=2\rho_0$, and its displacement from the event of $O$ at $\theta=0$ is $(2\rho_0,-\rho_0,0,0)$, with $\eta=-4\rho_0^2+\rho_0^2=-3\rho_0^2<0$ and positive time component, hence future timelike, so $q$ is causally after that event by [L5]; the displacement from the event of $O$ at $\theta=\log2$, namely $(\rho_0\sinh\log2,\rho_0\cosh\log2,0,0)=(\frac34\rho_0,\frac54\rho_0,0,0)$ by [L9], is $(5\rho_0/4,-5\rho_0/4,0,0)$, future null, so $q$ lies on a future null ray from $O$; but $V(q)=2\rho_0\ge0$, so by the criterion $q$ cannot reach any event of $O$ and receives no radar assignment, showing that the protocol does not extend even to events causally after $O$.

(Clause (iii): the limiting cases.) As $\rho_m\to0^+$ we have $|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|\to+\infty$ by strict increase and unboundedness of $\log$ (equivalently $\log(\rho_0/\rho_m)\to+\infty$), so the round-trip proper time $(2\rho_0/c)|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ and the radar distance $\rho_0|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ grow without bound, while the reflector's proper acceleration $c^2/\rho_m\to+\infty$ by [L4]; as $\rho_m\to+\infty$ the same divergence of $|\log(\rho_m/\rho_0)|$ holds while $c^2/\rho_m\to0^+$.

(Clause (v): scope.) Every clause was computed from the adopted model and the cited mathematical suppliers; the several limiting cases (equal radii excluded, the degenerate $r=1$ value, the two null half-planes versus the full horizon planes, the two limiting reflector radii) were treated explicitly. No apparatus, measurement, statistical or empirical input enters, no choice principle was used, and the statements are conditional model computations.

boundaries.reason: The theorem concerns a fixed congruence worldline and a fixed reflector radius; no possibly empty family is quantified over, and the protocol's triple is required to exist.

reviewed.reason: The congruence fixes positive observer radius and, for radar, a positive distinct reflector radius. Its family is parameterized by the explicit nonempty right wedge; existence of emission/reflection/reception is proved by monotone null coordinates, rather than inferred from an empty aggregate.

boundaries.evidence: Zero values are treated: U<0<V on the left wedge and U=V=0 only at the apex in step 1.1, and the coincident-radius case rho_m=rho_0 is excluded in step 3.3 by hypothesis.
The one-circuit-style uniqueness of the emission, reflection and reception events is proved in step 2.3; a single congruence worldline O and one reflector are the subject.

The degenerate cases are the equal radii rho_m=rho_0 (excluded; step 3.3) and the limiting radii rho_m->0 and rho_m->infinity, treated in step 4.1; the horizon planes are treated in steps 1.1 and 2.2.
The limit behaviour at the chart boundary rho=0 (the horizon, infinite radar distance) and as rho_m->infinity is addressed in step 2.2 and step 4.1.
Step 5.1 records that no choice principle is used; the criteria are proved constructively for each event.
Step 2.1 (from step 1.4) proves: if q<=p for some p on O then V(q)<0, and if p<=q then U(q)>0.
Step 1.4 also proves the converse criteria: V(q)<0 gives a reachable event p on O by an explicit choice of theta_p, and U(q)>0 symmetrically.

citations.quote:
Adopt [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] and [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] ($x^0 = c t$). Let $x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be the chart of an inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Fix $R > 0$, a real $\Omega$ with $|\Omega| R < c$, a real $x^3_0$ and a real $\phi_0$, and put $\gamma := (1 - \Omega^2 R^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. A rigidly rotating circular ring of radius $R$ and height $x^3_0$ about the $x^3$-axis, with angular velocity $\Omega$, has material worldlines

$$W_{\phi_0}(t) := x^{-1}(c t,\; R \cos(\phi_0 + \Omega t),\; R \sin(\phi_0 + \Omega t),\; x^3_0),\qquad t \in \mathbb R.$$

(i) **The ring worldline and the ring congruence.** $W_{\phi_0}$ is a $C^\infty$ future timelike worldline with unit observer

$$n = \gamma\,\bigl(1,\;-(\Omega R/c)\sin(\phi_0+\Omega t),\;(\Omega R/c)\cos(\phi_0+\Omega t),\;0\bigr) = (\gamma/c)\,\partial_t|_{\varphi},$$

$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and four-velocity $U = c n = \gamma\,\partial_t|_{\varphi}$, $\eta(U,U) = -c^2$, where $\varphi := \phi - \Omega t$ is the rotating angular label of the ring material points; it is an unparametrized flow line of the rigid-rotation congruence $n = \gamma(r)\,[\partial_0 + (\Omega/c)(-x^2\partial_1 + x^1\partial_2)]$ restricted to $r = R$, and its proper time $\tau$ and the chart time $t$ satisfy $d\tau = dt/\gamma$, so $\tau = t/\gamma + \tau_0$ for an arbitrary proper-time origin $\tau_0$ on this worldline ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] (c), [[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]).

(ii) **The guided-signal model.** Adopt, as an explicit model assumption of an ideal circular guide attached to the ring and of the signal and detector model below, and not as a consequence of the postulates: two ideal signals are emitted at the common emission event $W_{\phi_0}(0)$ into the guide, one in the positive angular direction and one in the negative angular direction (respectively co-rotating and counter-rotating for $\Omega > 0$, with these roles reversed for $\Omega < 0$), and in the inertial chart they follow the curves $C_+$ and $C_-$ given by $\phi_+(t) = \phi_0 + c t/R$ and $\phi_-(t) = \phi_0 - c t/R$ with radius $R$ and height $x^3_0$, i.e. each guided signal has chart angular rate $+c/R$ or $-c/R$ along the guide ('inertial tangential speed $c$ along the guide'); the detector is an ideal clock carried by the ring material point labelled $\varphi = \phi_0$. Each of $C_+$ and $C_-$ is a future null curve of the chart: its tangent has time component $c$ and spatial part of Euclidean length $c$, so the tangent has $\eta$-norm $0$ and positive time component ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

(iii) **Return times and differences.** The displayed guided curves have all-real mathematical extensions; emitted signals are their restrictions $t \ge 0$. On those extensions $C_+$ meets the worldline $W_{\phi_0}$ exactly at the chart times $2 \pi k R/(c - \Omega R)$, $k \in \mathbb Z$, and $C_-$ exactly at the chart times $2 \pi k R/(c + \Omega R)$, $k \in \mathbb Z$; the smallest positive meeting times are $t_1 := 2 \pi R/(c - \Omega R) > 0$ and $t_2 := 2 \pi R/(c + \Omega R) > 0$. Hence the two counter-propagating signals emitted at the same event reunite with the emitting material point at the reception events $W_{\phi_0}(t_1)$ and $W_{\phi_0}(t_2)$, each having gained exactly one circuit relative to that material point, and the chart-time difference of the two reunions is $t_1 - t_2 = 4 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2 R^2) > 0$ for $\Omega > 0$. The proper-time difference measured by the detector ideal clock is $(t_1 - t_2)/\gamma = 4 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 \sqrt{1 - \Omega^2R^2/c^2})$. For $\Omega = 0$ (inertial ring) $t_1 = t_2 = 2 \pi R/c$ and both differences vanish; for $\Omega < 0$ the sign of the first difference reverses and the roles of $C_+$ and $C_-$ are interchanged.

(iv) **Relation to the ring rest-synchronization holonomy.** On the fixed-height timelike cylinder $C = \{r = R,\ x^3 = x^3_0\}$, material worldlines have constant rotating label. Its rest lines instead vary $\varphi$ on an angular lift and satisfy $dt/d\varphi = \Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2R^2)$, being integral curves of $\partial_\varphi + [\Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2R^2)]\,\partial_t$; for $\Omega = 0$ they are $t = \text{constant}$ circles; one circuit $\varphi \to \varphi + 2 \pi$ has the chart-time holonomy $\Delta t_h = 2 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2R^2) = (t_1 - t_2)/2$ and the receiver proper-time holonomy $\Delta \tau_h = \Delta t_h/\gamma = 2 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 \sqrt{1 - \Omega^2R^2/c^2}) = (1/2)(t_1 - t_2)/\gamma$, exactly half of the detector proper-time difference of (iii); for $\Omega = 0$ both holonomies vanish. The ambient three-dimensional rest distribution of the rotating congruence is nowhere integrable for $\Omega \neq 0$, so no ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists, while the one-dimensional rest distribution restricted to the fixed-height cylinder $C$ is locally integrable and has the global holonomy just computed, nonvanishing exactly when $\Omega \neq 0$; the return-time computation of (iii) uses only the guided null curves and the material worldline and does not use either integrability property ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] (c), [[thm-sr-local-congruence-adapted-charts-and-frobenius]]).

(v) **Scope.** All quantities are conditional model computations for the specified ring, guide, signal and detector idealizations. The guided-signal curves are an adopted device model: the ideal vacuum light rays of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] are straight future null lines and do not circulate around the ring by themselves, and no assertion is made about optical fibers, refractive media, dispersion, absorption, finite resolution, apparatus calibration, interference phase or wave optics, or about one-way synchronization conventions between distinct ring observers; no measurement outcome, statistical inference or empirical claim is made, the values of $R$ and $\Omega$ are parameters and not measured quantities, and no choice principle is used.

Let $x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be the chart of an inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Fix $R > 0$, a real $\Omega$ with $|\Omega| R < c$, a real $x^3_0$ and a real $\phi_0$, and put $\gamma := (1 - \Omega^2 R^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. A rigidly rotating circular ring of radius $R$ and height $x^3_0$ about the $x^3$-axis, with angular velocity $\Omega$, has material worldlines

$$W_{\phi_0}(t) := x^{-1}(c t,\; R \cos(\phi_0 + \Omega t),\; R \sin(\phi_0 + \Omega t),\; x^3_0),\qquad t \in \mathbb R.$$

(i) **The ring worldline and the ring congruence.** $W_{\phi_0}$ is a $C^\infty$ future timelike worldline with unit observer

$$n = \gamma\,\bigl(1,\;-(\Omega R/c)\sin(\phi_0+\Omega t),\;(\Omega R/c)\cos(\phi_0+\Omega t),\;0\bigr) = (\gamma/c)\,\partial_t|_{\varphi},$$

$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and four-velocity $U = c n = \gamma\,\partial_t|_{\varphi}$, $\eta(U,U) = -c^2$, where $\varphi := \phi - \Omega t$ is the rotating angular label of the ring material points; it is an unparametrized flow line of the rigid-rotation congruence $n = \gamma(r)\,[\partial_0 + (\Omega/c)(-x^2\partial_1 + x^1\partial_2)]$ restricted to $r = R$, and its proper time $\tau$ and the chart time $t$ satisfy $d\tau = dt/\gamma$, so $\tau = t/\gamma + \tau_0$ for an arbitrary proper-time origin $\tau_0$ on this worldline ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] (c), [[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]).

Each of $C_+$ and $C_-$ is a future null curve of the chart: its tangent has time component $c$ and spatial part of Euclidean length $c$, so the tangent has $\eta$-norm $0$ and positive time component ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

(iii) **Return times and differences.** The displayed guided curves have all-real mathematical extensions; emitted signals are their restrictions $t \ge 0$. On those extensions $C_+$ meets the worldline $W_{\phi_0}$ exactly at the chart times $2 \pi k R/(c - \Omega R)$, $k \in \mathbb Z$, and $C_-$ exactly at the chart times $2 \pi k R/(c + \Omega R)$, $k \in \mathbb Z$; the smallest positive meeting times are $t_1 := 2 \pi R/(c - \Omega R) > 0$ and $t_2 := 2 \pi R/(c + \Omega R) > 0$. Hence the two counter-propagating signals emitted at the same event reunite with the emitting material point at the reception events $W_{\phi_0}(t_1)$ and $W_{\phi_0}(t_2)$, each having gained exactly one circuit relative to that material point, and the chart-time difference of the two reunions is $t_1 - t_2 = 4 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2 R^2) > 0$ for $\Omega > 0$. The proper-time difference measured by the detector ideal clock is $(t_1 - t_2)/\gamma = 4 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 \sqrt{1 - \Omega^2R^2/c^2})$. For $\Omega = 0$ (inertial ring) $t_1 = t_2 = 2 \pi R/c$ and both differences vanish; for $\Omega < 0$ the sign of the first difference reverses and the roles of $C_+$ and $C_-$ are interchanged.

(iv) **Relation to the ring rest-synchronization holonomy.** On the fixed-height timelike cylinder $C = \{r = R,\ x^3 = x^3_0\}$, material worldlines have constant rotating label. Its rest lines instead vary $\varphi$ on an angular lift and satisfy $dt/d\varphi = \Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2R^2)$, being integral curves of $\partial_\varphi + [\Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2R^2)]\,\partial_t$; for $\Omega = 0$ they are $t = \text{constant}$ circles; one circuit $\varphi \to \varphi + 2 \pi$ has the chart-time holonomy $\Delta t_h = 2 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 - \Omega^2R^2) = (t_1 - t_2)/2$ and the receiver proper-time holonomy $\Delta \tau_h = \Delta t_h/\gamma = 2 \pi \Omega R^2/(c^2 \sqrt{1 - \Omega^2R^2/c^2}) = (1/2)(t_1 - t_2)/\gamma$, exactly half of the detector proper-time difference of (iii); for $\Omega = 0$ both holonomies vanish. The ambient three-dimensional rest distribution of the rotating congruence is nowhere integrable for $\Omega \neq 0$, so no ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists, while the one-dimensional rest distribution restricted to the fixed-height cylinder $C$ is locally integrable and has the global holonomy just computed, nonvanishing exactly when $\Omega \neq 0$; the return-time computation of (iii) uses only the guided null curves and the material worldline and does not use either integrability property ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] (c), [[thm-sr-local-congruence-adapted-charts-and-frobenius]]).

(v) **Scope.** All quantities are conditional model computations for the specified ring, guide, signal and detector idealizations. The guided-signal curves are an adopted device model: the ideal vacuum light rays of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] are straight future null lines and do not circulate around the ring by themselves, and no assertion is made about optical fibers, refractive media, dispersion, absorption, finite resolution, apparatus calibration, interference phase or wave optics, or about one-way synchronization conventions between distinct ring observers; no measurement outcome, statistical inference or empirical claim is made, the values of $R$ and $\Omega$ are parameters and not measured quantities, and no choice principle is used.

**(a) Preservation.** Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline and let $X,Y:I\to V$ be $C^1$ Fermi–Walker transported fields along $x$ ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]]). Then $\tau\mapsto\eta(X(\tau),Y(\tau))$ is constant on $I$; in particular Fermi–Walker transport preserves norms and orthogonality, and the unique Fermi–Walker transported family with initial values a tetrad $(E_0(\tau_0),\dots,E_3(\tau_0))$ with $E_0(\tau_0)=U(\tau_0)/c$ is an orthonormal tetrad $(E_0(\tau),\dots,E_3(\tau))$ at every $\tau$ with $E_0(\tau)=U(\tau)/c$ (observer-adapted tetrad), by [[lem-sr-fermi-walker-transport-existence-and-uniqueness]].

**(b) Rindler wedge congruence.** In an inertial chart $(x^0,x,y,z)$ consider $\Phi(\theta,\rho,y,z):=(\rho\sinh\theta,\rho\cosh\theta,y,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$, with $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\rho>0$. Then $\Phi$ is a smooth bijection onto the right wedge $W:=\{(x^0,x):x>|x^0|\}$, with smooth inverse $\rho=\sqrt{x^2-(x^0)^2}$, $\theta=\tfrac12\log\bigl((x+x^0)/(x-x^0)\bigr)$ ([[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]], [[def-hyperbolic-functions]]); the pullback of $\eta$ is $g=-\rho^2d\theta^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$; the field $n:=\rho^{-1}\partial/\partial\theta$ is a future unit timelike field on $W$ whose congruence is Born rigid and irrotational, with acceleration $a=\nabla_nn=\rho^{-1}\partial/\partial\rho$, hence $\eta(a,a)=\rho^{-2}$; its rest slices $\theta=const$ are hyperplanes orthogonal to $n$ with induced metric $d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$ independent of $\theta$; and the frame $(n,\partial/\partial\rho,\partial/\partial y,\partial/\partial z)$ is a tetrad field which is not a coordinate frame, since $[n,\partial/\partial\rho]=+(1/\rho)n$ is nonzero ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]).

**(c) Rigid rotation, ambient nonintegrability and ring holonomy.** Fix real $\Omega$. In the inertial chart let $U_\Omega$ be the open timelike region $r^2=(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2<c^2/\Omega^2$ when $\Omega\ne0$, and the whole chart when $\Omega=0$. On this four-dimensional open set put $K=\partial_0+(\Omega/c)(-x^2\partial_1+x^1\partial_2)$, $\gamma(r)=(1-\Omega^2r^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and $n=\gamma(r)K$. This is a smooth future unit timelike Born-rigid congruence. If $\Omega\ne0$, its three-dimensional rest distribution in the ambient open set is nowhere integrable: its vorticity is nowhere zero and no ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists locally. If $\Omega=0$, $n=\partial_0$ is inertial and irrotational, and the rest hypersurfaces are $x^0=const$. Now fix $R>0$ with $|\Omega|R<c$ and restrict to the timelike ring cylinder $r=R$, $x^3=const$, whose rotating angle is $\varphi=\phi-\Omega t$ modulo $2\pi$, with $x^0=ct$. The ring observer $\phi=\phi_0+\Omega t$ has $n=\gamma(R)\bigl(1,-(\Omega R/c)\sin\phi,(\Omega R/c)\cos\phi,0\bigr)$. The induced metric is $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)dt^2+2\Omega R^2\,dt\,d\varphi+R^2d\varphi^2$. The ambient rest covector restricted to the cylinder is proportional to $-(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)dt+\Omega R^2d\varphi$, so the one-dimensional rest distribution on that cylinder is locally integrable and satisfies $dt/d\varphi=\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)$. After one positive circuit in the rotating label, its lift starting at $t=0$ has signed time offset $\Delta t=2\pi\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)$. For $\Omega\ne0$ it returns to the same rotating label at a different time and does not close as a ring rest-simultaneity curve; there is no globally single-valued real rest-synchronization time on the entire cylinder with time-oriented nonzero differential annihilating these rest lines. This global ring holonomy is distinct from the ambient local Frobenius obstruction. For $\Omega=0$ the offset is zero and ring rest lines are $t=const$.

**(d) Bell first-order field.** Let $q:J\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$ with $q(t)=(q_1(t),0,0)$ and $|q_1'(t)|<c$, and consider the $C^1$ future unit field of the translated worldlines $x_\xi(t)=(ct,q(t)+\xi)$ parametrized by $\xi$ in an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, with $n=\gamma\bigl(1,q_1'(t)/c,0,0\bigr)$, $\gamma=(1-q_1'(t)^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and unit longitudinal rest vector $s=\gamma\bigl(q_1'(t)/c,1,0,0\bigr)$. For this $C^1$ field define the first-order rest projection $h^a{}_b=\delta^a{}_b+n^an_b$ and projected deformation $\theta_{ab}=h^c{}_ah^d{}_b\partial_{(c}n_{d)}$, using the explicit first-order version of [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]. These coordinate formulas need only $C^1$ $n$, give a continuous tensor, and agree with the smooth congruence definitions when $q$ is smooth; in this first-order sense Born rigidity means $\theta=0$. Then

$$\theta(s,s)=s^as^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3q_1'(t)q_1''(t)/c^3,$$

which is nonzero exactly when $q_1'(t)q_1''(t)$ is nonzero; hence the congruence is not Born rigid on any neighbourhood of a parameter value with $q_1'(t)q_1''(t)\ne0$, although for every fixed chart time $t$ the separation between the members labelled $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ is the constant $|\xi_1-\xi_2|$. A breaking or fracture conclusion about a material rod would additionally require an elasticity model and a failure criterion and is not a kinematic statement.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ consisting of the following four pieces of data.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.
